report:
Conclusion: the blanket claim is **not supported as a general causal statement**. Evidence is observational and mixed: some cohorts show lower ischemic-heart-disease risk among vegetarians, but consistent all-cause mortality/life-expectancy gains are not proven.

The Adventist Health Study 2 reported lower mortality for several vegetarian patterns, especially in men, but participants were Seventh-day Adventists—an unusually health-conscious population—limiting generalizability (https://jamanetwork.com/journals/jamainternalmedicine/fullarticle/1710093). EPIC-Oxford found vegetarians had lower ischemic heart disease than meat eaters, yet higher hemorrhagic and total stroke, showing trade-offs rather than simple longevity benefit (https://www.bmj.com/content/366/bmj.l4897). A meta-analysis concluded vegetarian diets were associated with reduced ischemic-heart-disease mortality but **no effect on all-cause or cerebrovascular mortality** (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632/). In Australia’s 45 and Up cohort, researchers found **no mortality difference** between vegetarians and non-vegetarians after adjustment (https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0091743516304479).

Overall, vegetarian diets can be healthy and may reduce some cardiovascular outcomes, but “increases life expectancy compared with eating meat” overstates the evidence. Apparent benefits are confounded by smoking, alcohol, exercise, income, BMI, and overall diet quality; meat quality and quantity also matter.
